DEPARTMENT 730 LAW AND MOTION RULINGS


Case Number: 23CHCV03727    Hearing Date: July 14, 2026    Dept: 730

Superior Court of California 

County of Los Angeles 

Department 730 

¿ 

20NINETEAM LLC, individually and derivatively on behalf of MOON POOL LLC, 

Plaintiff(s), 

vs. 

DUSTIN WOLFF, et al., 

Defendant(s). 

Case No.: 

23CHCV03727 

Hearing Date: 

July 14, 2026 

 

 

[TENTATIVE] ORDER RE: 

motion to be relieved as counsel 

 

I. BACKGROUND 

This is a derivative shareholder action arising from wrongful distributions from a limited liability company. (Compl., ¶ 21.) On December 5, 2023, Plaintiff filed its complaint against defendants Dustin Wolff, Stephanie Wolff, and DOEs 1 through 20, inclusive, and nominal defendant Moon Pool, LLC. The complaint asserts five causes of action for: (1) breach of fiduciary duty, (2) conversion, (3) accounting, (4) constructive trust, and (5) breach of covenant of good faith and fair dealing.  

The complaint alleges as follows:  

Plaintiff 20Nineteam, LLC (Plaintiff) holds a six percent ownership interest in Moon Pool, LLC. (Compl., ¶ 3.) Defendants Dustin Wolff (Dustin) and Stephanie Wolff (Stephanie) each owns a 20.8% interest in Moon Pool. (Compl., ¶ 4-5.) Dustin and Stephanie have been the sole managers of Moon Pool since July of 2022. (Compl., ¶ 7.) Between June 2020 and June 2022, Moon Pool made distributions totaling $2,520,000, and from July 2022 and November 2023 made at least $1,120,000 in ownership distributions to separate entities controlled or owned by Dustin and Stephanie, without making pro rata distributions to all members, including Plaintiff, in violation of the operating agreement. (Compl., ¶ 20-21.) Dustin and Stephanie’s conduct have jeopardized Moon Pool’s ability to conduct business and pay debts and distributions to members when due. (Compl., ¶ 23.)  

On March 2, 2026, Ropers Majeski, PC (Movant), counsel for Dustin, filed the present motion to be relieved as counsel.  

On April 21, 2026, the matter was called for hearing and continued to April 22, 2026, due to Movant’s non-appearance. The Court’s tentative ruling to deny the motion for lack of proof of service was not adopted. (Minute Order dated April 21, 2026.)  

On April 22, 2026, the present motion again came before the Court in Department 78 and was heard by Honorable Judge Tiana Murillo. The Court continued the hearing to May 29, 2026, due to deficiencies in the moving papers, and ordered Movant to personally serve the motion papers on Dustin and provide proof of personal service. (Minute Order dated April 22, 2026; Notice of Ruling dated April 23, 2026.)  

On May 21, 2026, the Court continued the hearing to June 23, 2026. 

On June 23, 2026, the Court continued the hearing once again, ordering Movant to personally serve the moving papers on Dustin and file proof of service.  

On June 29, 2026, Movant filed the Proof of Service. No opposition to the motion has been filed.  

Future hearing dates include a Case Management Conference on December 10, 2026; Final Status Conference on February 24, 2027, and Jury Trial on March 8, 2027.  

 

II. LEGAL STANDARD 

California Rule of Court rule 3.1362 (Motion to Be Relieved as Counsel) requires (1) notice of motion and motion to be directed to the client (made on the Notice of Motion and Motion to be Relieved as Counsel—Civil form (MC-051)); (2) a declaration stating in general terms and without compromising the confidentiality of the attorney-client relationship why a motion under Code of Civil Procedure section 284(2) is brought instead of filing a consent under Code of Civil Procedure section 284(1) (made on the Declaration in Support of Attorney's Motion to Be Relieved as Counsel—Civil form (MC-052)); (3) service of the notice of motion and motion and declaration on all other parties who have appeared in the case; and (4) the proposed order relieving counsel (prepared on the Order Granting Attorney's Motion to Be Relieved as Counsel—Civil form (MC-053)).  

The court has discretion to allow an attorney to withdraw, and such a motion should be granted provided that there is no prejudice to the client and it does not disrupt the orderly process of justice. (See Ramirez v. Sturdevant (1994) 21 Cal.App.4th 904, 915.) 

III. DISCUSSION 

Movant and all attorneys in the firm move to be relieved as counsel for Defendant Dustin. Movant has complied with the Court’s order to personally serve the defendant with moving papers and has filed the proof of service. No opposition has been filed. In addition, Dustin will not be prejudiced by the withdrawal because trial is in March 2027.  

Therefore, the Court grants the motion.  

IV. CONCLUSION 

The Motion to be Relieved is GRANTED.  

Ropers Majeski, PC, and its attorneys, shall be relieved as counsel upon filing of the proof of service of the signed order (MC-053).  

Moving Party is ordered to give notice. 

 

DATED: July 14, 2026 

__________________________ 

Hon. Alexander C.D. Giza 

Judge of the Superior Court

Case Number: 24STCV06620    Hearing Date: July 14, 2026    Dept: 730

Superior Court of California

County of Los Angeles

Department 730

 

JESSICA VALDIVIA,

Plaintiffs,

vs.

JACQUELINE SUZETTE, et al.

Defendants

Case No.:

24STCV06620

Hearing Date:

July 14, 2026

[TENTATIVE] ORDER GRANTING MOTION TO COMPEL RESPONSES TO REQUEST FOR PRODUCTION OF DOCUMENTS, SET ONE

 

I.                BACKGROUND

On March 18, 2024, Plaintiff (“Plaintiff”) Jessica Valdivia filed a complaint against Defendants Jacqueline Suzette, Juan Carlos Menjivar, Alfonso Rene Solano Ruiz, and Matheson Tri-Gas, Inc., alleging cause of action for negligence, arising out of an alleged vehicle collision.

 

On March 11, 2026, Defendant Matheson Tri-Gas, Inc. (“Defendant”) filed the instant motion to compel Plaintiff’s responses to Requests for Production of Documents, Set One (“RPDs”). Defendant also requests the Court impose sanctions of $1,060.00. No opposition has been filed.

 

II.             LEGAL STANDARD

A party must respond to interrogatories and requests for production within 30 days after service. (Code Civ. Proc., § 2031.260, subd. (a).) If a party to whom interrogatories and requests for production are directed does not provide timely responses, the requesting party may move for an order compelling responses to the discovery. (Code Civ. Proc., § 2031.300, subd. (b).)

 

“The court may impose a monetary sanction ordering that one engaging in the misuse of the discovery process, or any attorney advising that conduct, or both pay the reasonable expenses, including attorney’s fees, incurred by anyone as a result of that conduct.” (Code Civ. Proc. § 2023.030, subd. (a).) Misuse of the discovery process includes: “(d) failing to respond or¿to submit to an authorized method of discovery.” (Code Civ. Proc. § 2023.010, subd. (d).) Reasonable expenses under Code of Civil Procedure section 2023.030, subdivision (a) include the time spent in researching and preparing the motion, as well as court time and travel time spent in connection with the motion. (Ghanooni¿v. Super Shuttle¿(1993) 20 Cal.App.4th 256, 262.)
¿¿ 

III.           DISCUSSION

a.      Requests for Production of Documents

On December 5, 2025, Defendant served Plaintiff with written discovery consisting of Requests for Production of Documents, Set One. (Koumoulis Decl. ¶ 3, Exh. A.) Responses were due on February 26, 2026. (Ibid.) To date, no responses have been provided. (Id., ¶ 11.) As Defendant served Plaintiff with discovery requests and Plaintiff failed to provide responses, the motions are granted. Plaintiff is ordered to provide verified response without objections within 20 days of this order.

b.     Sanctions

Defendant seeks $1,060 in monetary sanctions against Plaintiff and her counsel. The Court relies on its knowledge and experience in determining the reasonable value of the legal services provided under the circumstances in this case, e.g., routine nature of the motion, concurrently filed motions, and lack of opposition. (In re Marriage of Huntington (1992) 10 Cal.App.4th 1513, 1524 [“When the trial court is informed of the extent and nature of the legal services rendered, it may rely on its own experience and knowledge in determining their reasonable value.”].) The Court has discretion to fix the amount of reasonable monetary sanctions. (Cornerstone Realty Advisors, LLC v. Summit Heatlthcare Reit, Inc. (2020) 56 Cal. App. 5th 771, 791.)

 

The Court finds a reasonable award is 2 hours of attorney’s work at a rate of $265 per hour.

 

Therefore, the Court imposes sanctions of $530 on Plaintiff and counsel of record, K. Christopher Ghahreman, jointly and severally, to be paid within 20 days of this order.

 

IV.           CONCLUSION

Defendant Matheson Tri-Gas, Inc.’s motion to compel Plaintiff Jessica Valdivia’s responses to Requests for Production of Documents, Set One, is GRANTED. Jessica Valdivia is ordered to provide verified, code-compliant, objection-free responses within 20 days of the hearing on the motion.

Defendant Matheson Tri-Gas, Inc.’s request for sanctions is GRANTED. Jessica Valdivia and counsel K. Christopher Ghahreman are ordered to pay $530 in sanctions to Matheson TriGas, Inc. within 20 days of the hearing on the motion.

Defendant is ordered to provide notice of this Order. 

 

DATED: July 14, 2026

__________________________

Hon. Alexander C.D. Giza

Judge of the Superior Court

Superior Court of California 

County of Los Angeles 

Department 730 

¿ 

JESSICA VALDIVIA, 

Plaintiff, 

vs. 

JACQUELINE SUZETTE, et al., 

Defendants 

Case No.: 

24STCV06620 

Hearing Date: 

July 14, 2026 

 

 

ORDER GRANTING UNOPPOSED MOTION TO DEEM REQUEST FOR ADMISSIONS ADMITTED 

 

Having reviewed Defendant Matheson Tri-Gas, Inc.’s unopposed Motion to Deem Requests for Admission Admitted, the Court rules as follows. 

On December 5, 2025, Defendant Matheson Tri-Gas, Inc. served Requests for Admission, Set No. One on Plaintiff Jessica Valdivia. 

Responses were due February 26, 2026. Plaintiff Jessica Valdivia has failed to provide timely responses. Defendant Matheson Tri-Gas, Inc. now moves the Court to deem the requests for admission admitted. No opposition has been filed. 

The Court grants the motion pursuant to Code of Civil Procedure section 2033.280 and deems the requests to be admitted.   

 

Defendant Matheson Tri-Gas, Inc. requests monetary sanctions pursuant to sections 2023.030 (a) and 2033.280 (c) in the amount of $1,060.00, based upon 4 hours of attorney’s work at a rate of $265.00 per hour, with 2 hours were spent drafting the motion and 2 hours are anticipated in reading and replying to any opposition. The Court finds the requested amount in sanctions unreasonable given this is an unopposed, routine discovery motion. (In re Marriage of Huntington (1992) 10 Cal.App.4th 1513, 1524 [“When the trial court is informed of the extent and nature of the legal services rendered, it may rely on its own experience and knowledge in determining their reasonable value.”].) Instead, a more reasonable award is $500.00, based upon 2 hours of attorney’s work at a reasonable rate of $265.00 per hour. Therefore, the Court imposes sanctions of $530.00. 

Therefore, the Court imposes sanctions totaling $530.00 and are payable by Plaintiff Jessica Valdivia and her counsel by August 13, 2026.

Case Number: 24STCV28664    Hearing Date: July 14, 2026    Dept: 730

Superior Court of California

County of Los Angeles

Department 730

 

JOSHUA GIL, et al.,

Plaintiff(s),

vs.

MATTHEW EGAN, et al.,

Defendant(s).

Case No.:

24STCV28664

Hearing Date:

July 14, 2026

[TENTATIVE] ORDER RE:

PETITION TO CONFIRM ARBITRATION AWARD

 

I.           BACKGROUND

Plaintiffs Joshua Gil (Gil) and Nice Yab Jeff LLC (NYJ) (collectively, “Plaintiffs”) filed their operative First Amended Complaint (FAC) against defendants Matthew Egan (Egan), Hola Restaurant LLC (HRL), Hola Comida III LLC (HCII), Hola Comida IV LLC (HCIV), Hola Comida Management LLC (HCM), Hola Comida Hospitality LLC (HCH), and Does 1 through 10, alleging the following.

After several conversations, Gil (a chef) and Egan (a creative producer, director, and editor of film and television) agreed to enter into a partnership to establish and operate restaurants in Los Angeles. (FAC ¶¶ 19, 20.) Egan would contribute money and general business acumen, and Gil would contribute his culinary skills and restaurant-specific knowledge. (FAC ¶ 20.) Gil was the primary force in coming up with the restaurant names, settling on Mirame, Mirate, and Miranos, which, in English, translate into Look at Me, Look at You, and Look at Us, respectively. (FAC ¶ 20.) Egan agreed. (FAC ¶ 20.)

The two individuals entered a Limited Partnership Agreement (hereinafter, the “LP Agreement”) to form a partnership called “Hola Comida I LP,” (Hola Comida I) whereby HRL would act as the General Partner and Gil would act as a Limited Partner of the partnership. (FAC ¶ 21.) Subsequent court filings attaching a copy of the LP Agreement show that the agreement was signed by Egan, as the authorized representative of HRL, and Gil in his personal capacity.

The LP Agreement included, among other things, equity divisions and the following prohibitions: (1) General and Limited Partners could not use “the name of the Partnership, or any substantially similar name, or any trademark or trade name adopted by the Partnership, except in the ordinary course of the Partnership’s business,” and (2) General Partner could not use “directly or indirectly, the assets of this Partnership for any purpose other than the carrying on the business of the Partnership, for the full and exclusive benefit of all its parties.” (FAC ¶ 22.)

However, Egan never intended to fulfill his part of the agreement, and instead leveraged Gil’s services as well as the assets, property, and goodwill created by Hola Comida I LP dba Mírame to establish other companies (HCH, HCM, HCII, and HCIV (collectively, the “Derivative Companies”) for his sole benefit, while neglecting and allowing HRL to be suspended by the Secretary of State. (FAC ¶ 28.)

Despite the suspension of HRL and creation of the Derivative Companies, Mírame continued to operate normally in tandem with Mírate until July 2, 2023, when Mírame ceased operations, and Egan represented to Gil that Gil had no equity or ownership in Mírate, despite previously telling Gil and representing to the public that Gil and Egan were partners in the operation of Mirate. (FAC ¶¶ 26-29.)

Thus, the FAC asserts causes of action for: (1) Breach of Written Contract, (2) Breach of Oral Contract, (3) Breach of Implied Covenant of Good Faith And Fair Dealing, (4) Breach of Fiduciary Duty, (5) Aiding And Abetting Breach of Fiduciary Duty, (6) Fraudulent Misrepresentation, (7) Fraudulent Concealment, (8) Fraudulent Inducement, (9) Statutory Claim For Improper Disposition of Property Or Services, and (10) Constructive Trust.

On January 17, 2025, Egan, HRL, and the Derivative Companies filed a motion to compel Gil’s lawsuit to arbitration pursuant to the arbitration clause in the LP Agreement. Plaintiffs opposed the motion.

On March 19, 2025, the Court granted the motion and compelled the parties to arbitration.  

On April 2, 2026, Gil filed his first Petition for Order Confirming Arbitration Award (the “First Petition”), seeking “an order confirming the March 18, 2026, arbitral award in his favor.” (4/2/26 First Petition, p. 1:4-5.)

On April 17, 2026, Egan, HRL, and the Derivative Companies (collectively, “Respondents”), opposed the First Petition, arguing, inter alia, that the First Petition was premature because the award was not final.

On April 30, 2026, the Court denied the First Petition without prejudice, agreeing with Respondents that the arbitration award was not yet final.

On May 7, 2026, Gil filed the instant Petition for Order Confirming Arbitration Award (the “Second Petition”), seeking an order confirming the “Final Award,” which is made of three rulings by the arbitrator:

1.     Interim award ruling of February 23, 2026 (5/7/26 Escalante Decl., Ex. C);

2.     Corrections ruling of March 19, 2026 (5/7/26 Escalante Decl., Ex. H); and

3.     Motion to Tax Costs ruling of April 16, 2026 (5/7/26 Escalante Decl., Ex. J).

(Second Petition, p. 2, fn. 1 [stating that the three components together “constitute the statutorily-defined final award because they were signed, served, and addressed all issues presented to the arbitrator. (See Cooper v. Lavely & Singer Professional Corp. (2014) 230 Cal.App.4th 1, 13 [noting the statutorily defined award may come in ‘multiple incremental awards’”].)      On May 18, 2026, Respondents filed their Response to the Second Petition.          On May 26, 2026, Gil filed his reply.

On June 2, 2026, the Court ordered the parties to file, by June 16, 2026, supplemental briefs addressing the following issues that were raised by the parties’ papers: “(1) Issue re reservation of exclusive jurisdiction [in a License Agreement introduced later in this ruling] vs. Arbitration Agreement [in the LP Agreement], and (2) Whether there is anything that prevented Defendant from filing a request for correction of the arbitration award [with regard to their contention that the arbitrator did not have the authority to award Gil royalties under or make any findings under the License Agreement].” (6/2/26 Minute Order, p. 1.)   On June 16, 2026, the parties filed their supplemental briefs.

On June 22, 2026, a Notice of Death and Substitution was filed notifying the Court that Gil had passed away on that date and that Mrs. Nellie Gil, Gil’s mother and trustee of the Joshua Misael Gil Irrevocable Trust, intends to substitute as plaintiff.          On June 30, 2026, the Court granted the parties’ stipulation to have Mrs. Gil (hereafter, “Petitioner”) substitute in Gil’s place.

 

II.         LEGAL STANDARD

“Any party to an arbitration in which an award has been made may petition the court to confirm, correct or vacate the award.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 1285.) Such a petition must set forth the substance, or attach copies of the arbitration agreement, award, and any written opinion. (Id., § 1285.4.) It must be served between 10 days and 4 years from the date the award was served on the petitioner. (Id., §§ 1288 & 1288.4.) The other party may respond to the petition. (Id., § 1285.2.)

“If a petition or response under this chapter is duly served and filed, the court shall confirm the award as made, whether rendered in this state or another state, unless in accordance with this chapter it corrects the award and confirms it as corrected, vacates the award or dismisses the proceeding.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 1286.) “If an award is confirmed, judgment shall be entered in conformity therewith.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 1287.4.)

The petition must: “(a) [s]et forth the substance of or have attached a copy of the agreement to arbitrate unless the petitioner denies the existence of such an agreement”; “(b) [s]et forth the names of the arbitrators” and “(c) [s]et forth or have attached a copy of the award and the written opinion of the arbitrators, if any.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 1285.4.) The petition must also “name as respondents all parties to the arbitration and may name as respondents any other persons bound by the arbitration award.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 1285.) A petition to confirm an award must be served and filed within four years after the date the petitioner was served with a signed copy of the award. (Code Civ. Proc., § 1288.)  

           

III.       DISCUSSION

The Second Petition asks the Court to confirm the Final Award and enter the following judgment in his favor:

1.     [Money judgment] in favor of Mr. Gil as follows:

                                   i.          $961,526.00 from Mr. Egan, HCIII, HCH, and HCM, jointly and severally;

                                  ii.          $112,103.10 [in royalty damages] from HCIV, HCH, and HCM, jointly and severally;   

                                iii.          [$16,232.99][1] from all Respondents, jointly and severally; and

                                iv.          $9,823.47 in post-Award, pre-judgment interest at the rate of seven percent (7%) per annum (equating to $209.01 per day) from April 16, 2026 through the date hereof.  

2.     The Limited Partnership Agreement, dated January 2020, and executed by both Mr. Gil and Mr. Egan, is binding on Mr. Gil and Mr. Egan; and

3.     The License Agreement is binding and, pursuant to that Agreement, Mr. Gil has a right to receive a royalty equal to 0.5% of the Gross Revenues received by the restaurants doing business as Daisy and Mirate until such time as the License Agreement is lawfully terminated.

(5/7/26 Proposed Order, p. 1:11-2:4.)

In their Response, Respondents ask the Court to vacate or correct the Final Award in part as follows.

1.     Deny the Second Petition as to the royalty components of the award and the requested declaratory relief;  

2.     Vacate the royalty damages of $112,103.10 under Code of Civil Procedure section 1286.2, subdivision (a)(4), on the grounds that the Arbitrator exceeded his powers by adjudicating rights under the License Agreement—a separate contract with an exclusive court jurisdiction clause, never submitted to arbitration, under which Gil is not the royalty obligee—and by awarding damages on a theory entirely absent from the First Amended Notice of Claims;

3.     Vacate the Mirate royalty correction of $82,518.48 under Code of Civil Procedure section 1286.2, subdivision (a)(5), as an independent and additional ground, on the basis that the royalty correction ruling issued two days before Respondents’ ARC Rule 19 opposition deadline—the same procedural defect the Arbitrator acknowledged in the companion cost ruling—and the April 16 Final Award contains no ruling on royalties;  

4.     Deny the request for declaratory relief affirming continuing royalty obligations under the License Agreement;  

5.     Confirm the LP interest award of $961,526 and the cost award of $16,232.99 and enter judgment thereon, with 7% post-award interest on those confirmed components from April 16, 2026; [and]

6.     In the alternative, correct the Award under Code of Civil Procedure section 1286.6, subdivision (a), to substitute the arithmetically correct HCM ownership percentage of 62.50%—derived from Trial Exhibit 218—for the 67.96% figure in the Award, reducing ownership-interest damages from $961,526 to $884,200 ….”

(Response, pp. 6:9-7:2.)

A.    Respondents’ Request to Vacate the “Royalties” Portion of the Final Award

Hola Comida I (as “Licensor”) and HCH (as “Licensee”) entered into a License Agreement on June 3, 2022, regarding the use and rights to the name, likeness, and other associated intellectual property of Egan and Gil (the “Chef Marks”), and regarding the use of the same for Mirame (the “Mirame Marks”). (5/7/26 Escalante Decl., Exh. C – a copy of the License Agreement, p. 1.)

The License Agreement stated: “With respect to the MÍRAME Marks and the CHEF Marks, Licensor shall be paid an annual royalty (‘Royalty’) equal to one percent (1.00%) of Gross Revenue of the Licensee’s Business from the Restaurants.” (License Agreement, § 7.A.) The term “Restaurants” was not defined in the agreement. The agreement only described the term as referring to “multiple restaurants” that were “to be developed” by Licensee. (See id. in the Recitals sections [“WHEREAS Licensee, directly and indirectly through one or more subsidiaries, desires to utilize the MÍRAME Marks and the CHEF Marks (together the ‘Marks’) in connection with the operation of multiple restaurant (the ‘Restaurants’) to be developed [by] Licensee (‘Business) …”].)

The arbitrator, Hon. Andrew C. Kauffman (Ret) (“Arbitrator”) found the following.

1.     The License Agreement was never terminated.

2.     Under the License agreement, Gil was entitled to royalties equaling 0.5 percent of the gross revenue of two restaurants, Mirate and Daisy.

3.     Based on expert testimony, the sum of those royalties for the two restaurants was $112,103.10.

(See 5/7/26 Escalante Decl., Exh. E -a copy of the Arbitrator’s 3/18/26 Ruling on Application for Correction of Award, p. 2 [“However, inasmuch as Daisy, as well as Mirate, is being operated by some combination of Hola Comida Hospitality and Rola Comida Management and no evidence was presented that the above Licensing Agreement with Rola Comida I was ever terminated, Gil remains entitled to his share of the provided royalty for licensed use of his Chef Marks. Otherwise, as there is no evidence that Rola Comida I has any ownership interest in these entities, no evidence that Gil was ever involved in the business of these entities and no evidence that Gil ever expressed any interest in participating in the ‘front of the house’ management of Mirame or Mirate, complainants’ ownership interest does not extend here. ¶ …. ¶ In determining these amounts, the expert testimony of Alstadt is conclusive. He notes that Egan has a 67.96% ownership interest in Rola Comida Hospitality, which owns 100% of Mirate. He opines that the present value of Mirate is $2,887,430 as of December 31, 2025, and that the value of 49% of Egan's ownership interest is $961,526. Additionally, based upon actual and projected revenue, Alstadt opines that the gross revenue for Mirate for years 2024 and 2025 is $8,378,640 and $8,125,056, respectively, and that the annualized gross revenue for Daisy’s first year of operation is $5,916,923. Each of these opinions is supported by his review of all related financial records. No conflicting evidence or opinion is presented. ¶ …. ¶ Accordingly, as against Egan, Hola Comida III, Hola Comida Hospitality, and Hola Comida Management, I award complainants damages in the amount of $961,526. Having calculated that one-half of one percent of $8,378,640 is $41,893.20; that one-half of one percent of $8,125.056 is $40,625.28; and that one-half percent of $5,916,923 is $29,584.62, I award those additional damages, totaling $112,103.10, against Hola Comida IV, Hola Comida Hospitality, and Hola Comida Management to Gil only”].)

Respondents now argue that the Arbitrator exceeded his powers in awarding Gil the royalties for the following reasons:

a.      “The License Agreement was never submitted to arbitration.  No party filed claims under it, no stipulation extended the arbitration to encompass it, and it was introduced at the evidentiary hearing solely as documentary background evidence;

b.     The License Agreement is a separate contract from both versions of the LP Agreement—executed more than two years after the January 2020 LPA, between different parties (Hola Comida I, LP as Licensor and Hola Comida Hospitality LLC as Licensee)—and neither version of the LP Agreement's arbitration clause encompasses disputes arising under it;

c.      Section 22 of the License Agreement affirmatively withdraws License Agreement disputes from arbitration, providing that the courts of Los Angeles County ‘shall have exclusive jurisdiction to hear and decide all controversies that may arise under or concerning this Agreement’;                

d.     The First Amended Notice of Claims—the operative pleading defining the scope of the arbitration—contains no cause of action under the License Agreement, no factual allegation that any royalties are owed to Mr. Gil, and no prayer for royalty damages.  The word ‘royalty’ does not appear.  An arbitrator lacks authority to award damages on a theory the parties never submitted;

e.      Section 7(A) of the License Agreement identifies the royalty obligee as Hola Comida I, LP, not Mr. Gil personally.  Mr. Gil's only path to any portion of those royalties was through his 49% LP interest—the same interest already fully compensated in the $961,526 ownership-interest award.  Awarding direct royalties on top of that award constitutes impermissible double recovery; and

f.      The prospective declaratory relief requested in the Second Petition— affirming Mr. Gil's right to receive 0.5% of Gross Revenues at Daisy and Mirate until the License Agreement "is lawfully terminated"—would enforce a contract with an exclusive court jurisdiction clause that was never before the Arbitrator.”

 

(5/18/26 Response to Second Petition, p. 4:4-28.)

In the reply, Petitioner argues that the Arbitrator did not exceed his powers for the following reasons.

First, the royalties issue fell within the scope of the arbitration clause of the LP Agreement. (See 5/7/26 Escalante Decl., Exh A – a copy of the LP Agreement § 14.4 [“All Parties agree to resolve any claim or dispute arising under or relating to this Agreement or the business and purpose intended hereunder, through binding arbitration”]; 5/26/26 Reply, pp. 2:26-3:3 [“First, the arbitration agreement pulls in any claim or dispute ‘arising under or relating to’ the ‘business and purpose intended hereunder.’ [Citation.] Damages awarded based on the value of a License Agreement signed by the partnership (Hola Comida I LP) and in furtherance of the partnership that Mr. Egan wrongfully repudiated is manifestly a claim or dispute ‘arising under or relating to’ the business of the partnership”].)

 

Second, the Arbitrator had broad, equitable authority to award damages he saw fit. (5/26/26 Reply, p. 3:14-20.)

Third, “Respondents raised these arguments prior to issuance of the Final Award and, by not revisiting [his] interim ruling on this point, the Arbitrator has rejected these arguments.” (5/26/26 Reply, p. 4:11-14.) Specifically, “The Arbitrator’s interim ruling, issued on February 23, awarded royalties. (Escalante Decl., Ex. C.) On March 5, Mr. Gil requested additional royalties and costs. (Escalante Decl., ¶ 9.) The Arbitrator issued additional rulings on March 19, 2026, addressing the request for additional royalties and costs. (Escalante Decl., Ex. H.) Only then did Respondents raise an objection to both the award of costs and royalties. (Escalante Decl., ¶ 12.) The Arbitrator withdrew the award on costs as premature (Escalante Decl., Ex. I), which the Court previously found appropriate over Mr. Gil’s objection, and the Arbitrator issued a new award on costs. (Escalante Decl., Exs. Accordingly, for that period of time when the Arbitrator was reconsidering the cost award, it was purportedly free from limitation on any changes. [Citation.] Nevertheless, despite Respondents’ request to reconsider the royalties, the Arbitrator made no change to the ruling on royalties. Accordingly, the Arbitrator’s Final Award implicitly reaffirmed the rejection of Respondents’ arguments.” (Id. at p. 4:14-28.)

              Fourth, “the award of damages based on unpaid royalties is not an inappropriate double recovery.” (5/26/26 Reply, P. 5:12-13.)

Fifth, the royalty issue is not a “jurisdictional” issue; it is a damages issue and relief issue, which the Arbitrator considered and ruled upon. (5/26/26 Reply, p. 6:1-7.)

In the supplemental brief and connected to the third point above, Petitioner argues that Respondents waived their royalties dispute by failing to submit it to the Arbitrator in the first instance. (6/16/26 Supplemental Brief in Support of Second Petition, p. 5:3-4.)

The Court finds Petitioner’s argument that the arbitration clause in the LP Agreement encompassed the License Agreement issue unpersuasive. Granted, “‘[b]road contractual provisions for arbitration [such as the one in the LP Agreement] are to be liberally construed.’ [Citation.]” (Bigler v. Harker School (2013) 213 Cal.App.4th 727, 738.) However, “[a]rbitration is strictly a matter of consent. A party cannot be required to arbitrate a dispute that he or she has not agreed to submit to arbitration.” (Duran v. EmployBridge Holding Co. (2023) 92 Cal.App.5th 59, 65.) “[I]nterpretation of the arbitration agreement employs the ordinary rules of contract interpretation. [Citation.] Our goal is to give effect to the mutual intention of the parties at the time the contract was formed.” (Duran v. EmployBridge Holding Co. (2023) 92 Cal.App.5th 59, 65.) “Under California law, the first step in analyzing the meaning of a contract is to determine whether the language is ambiguous—that is, reasonably susceptible to more than one meaning.” (Id. at p. 66.) When the parties to an arbitration agreement indicate the agreement is ambiguous by disputing its meaning of a contract but fail to present extrinsic evidence in support of their arguments, California courts “resolve the question of ambiguity based solely on the contents of their agreement.” (Ibid.) Here, the Court finds that there is nothing in the LP Agreement that indicates that the parties bound by that agreement intended to arbitrate their dispute regarding the License Agreement. Indeed, the LP Agreement was executed on January 2, 2020, by HRL and Gil, while the License Agreement was executed approximately two years later in June 2022, and by different parties, Hola Comida I and HCH. Therefore, Petitioner’s argument that the scope of the arbitration clause in the LP Agreement covered disputes under the License Agreement is unpersuasive.

Petitioner’s other arguments, that the Arbitrator had broad authority to award Gil the royalties and that Respondents waived their right to dispute that award by refusing to contest that part of the award in front of the Arbitrator, are also unpersuasive for the following reasons.

As Respondents allude to in their supplemental brief, Code of Civil Procedure section 1284 (“Section 1284”) did not give the Arbitrator the authority to reconsider his interim ruling on the ground that he exceeded his powers. Section 1284 states: “The arbitrators, upon written application of a party to the arbitration, may correct the award upon any of the grounds set forth in subdivisions (a) and (c) of Section 1286.6 not later than 30 days after service of a signed copy of the award on the applicant” (emphasis added). Section 1286.6 in turn states: “Subject to Section 1286.8, the court, unless it vacates the award pursuant to Section 1286.2, shall correct the award and confirm it as corrected if the court determines that: ¶ (a) There was an evident miscalculation of figures or an evident mistake in the description of any person, thing or property referred to in the award; ¶ (b) The arbitrators exceeded their powers but the award may be corrected without affecting the merits of the decision upon the controversy submitted; or ¶ (c) The award is imperfect in a matter of form, not affecting the merits of the controversy” (italics added). Therefore, because Section 1284 did not allow the Arbitrator to reconsider his interim ruling under subdivision (b) of Section 1286.8, it would have been futile for Respondents to challenge the interim ruling on the basis that the Arbitrator exceeded his powers regarding the License Agreement issue.

Granted, courts “give ‘substantial deference to the arbitrator[’s] own assessments of [his] contractual authority.’ [Citation.]” (California Union Square L.P. v. Saks & Co. LLC (2020) 50 Cal.App.5th 340, 349.)

In addition, unless the parties’ contract or an agreed submission to arbitration explicitly and unambiguously limits an arbitrator’s powers, the arbitrator may base his decision upon broad principles of justice and equity. (See Cable Connection, Inc. v. DIRECTV, Inc. (2008) 44 Cal.4th 1334, 1355 [“‘“Arbitrators, unless specifically required to act in conformity with rules of law, may base their decision upon broad principles of justice and equity, and in doing so may expressly or impliedly reject a claim that a party might successfully have asserted in a judicial action.’ [Citations.]’ [Citation]”]; J.C. Gury, supra, 152 Cal.App.4th at p. 1305 [“‘An exception to the general rule assigning broad powers to the arbitrators arises when the parties have, in either the contract or an agreed submission to arbitration, explicitly and unambiguously limited those powers. [Citation.] “The powers of an arbitrator derive from, and are limited by, the agreement to arbitrate. [Citation.] Awards in excess of those powers may, under sections 1286.2and 1286.6, be corrected or vacated by the court.” [Citation.]’ [Citation]”].)

Here, there is no evidence that anything in the arbitration provision in the LP Agreement or the parties’ pleadings in the arbitration explicitly and unambiguously limited the Arbitrator from determining the License Agreement issue.

However, as explained above, arbitration is a matter of contract, and there is no evidence that the parties agreed to arbitrate the License Agreement issue.

The Court also finds that this case is unlike others in which the Court of Appeal held a party waived a limitation on the scope of arbitration.

In J.C. Gury, for example, the Court of Appeal found that the parties’ arbitration clause expressly limited the arbitrator’s power to modify or alter the terms of the contract. (J.C. Gury, supra, 152 Cal.App.4th at p. 1304.) The arbitration clause stated: “‘Scope of Power: In any arbitration proceeding arising under this Contract, the arbitrators shall not have the power to change, modify or alter any expressed condition, term or provision of this Contract or to grant an award which has such effect, and to that extent the scope of their authority is so limited.’” (Id. at p. 1305.) The arbitrator in that case issued an award finding a contract clause unconscionable, a finding that necessarily implicated the limitation in the arbitration clause. (Ibid. [“In this case, it is difficult to disagree with the proposition that an arbitral finding that a contract provision is unconscionable and unenforceable necessarily effects a change or alteration in that provision, within the meaning of the parties’ arbitration clause. Certainly an award founded on the conclusion a contractual provision is unenforceable ‘has [the] effect’ of ‘chang[ing], modify[ing] or alter[ing]’ that provision of the contract”].)

Despite finding that the arbitration award implicated the limitation provision in the arbitration clause, the Court of Appeal concluded that the arbitrator did not exceed his powers by deciding the unconscionability issue because the appellant had waived enforcing the limitation provision in the following ways.

First, the appellant was aware of the appellee’s unconscionability argument before the arbitration. (See J.C. Gury, supra, 152 Cal.App.4th at p. 1306 [“Before the arbitration, Gury [the appellee] and Nippon Carbide [the appellant] submitted briefs for the arbitrator’s consideration. Gury devoted almost half of its brief to its contention that the warranty disclaimer in the contract was unenforceable and unconscionable. In reply, Nippon Carbide argued that ‘no basis exist[ed] for refusing to enforce’ its warranty disclaimer. It distinguished precedents cited by Gury, and cited precedent rejecting claims that a contract's warranty disclaimer and damages limitation were unconscionable”].)

Second, “at no time [during the arbitration did the appellant] ‘remind[] the arbitrator’ of the contractual limitation on the scope of his authority in the arbitration clause of the contract,” nor “cite[d] to any evidence, pleading or argument in the record showing it ever suggested to the arbitrator that he had no authority to find the warranty clause unconscionable or to refuse to enforce it.” (Ibid.) “[T]he record [there] support[ed] only one conclusion: that both parties unequivocally submitted the issue of unconscionability to arbitration. Having done so, [the appellant could] … not now complain that the arbitrator exceeded his authority.” (Ibid.)

Here, unlike J.C. Gury, Petitioner has not presented any evidence that (1) Respondents were aware that the License Agreement issue was “submitted” to the Arbitrator (e.g., through Gil’s claim for arbitration), and (2) Respondents waived the right to enforce the exclusive jurisdiction clause in the License Agreement by failing to challenge Gil’s pleadings seeking adjudication of issues under that agreement.

Therefore, the Court concludes that the Arbitrator acted in excess of his authority when he made rulings regarding the License Agreement issue, including awarding Gil royalty interests in Mirate and Daisy restaurants.

Accordingly, Respondents’ request to sever the royalty and License Agreement portion of the Final Award is GRANTED. In light of that conclusion, the parties’ arguments regarding whether the royalty portion of the award constitutes double recovery and whether Respondents were given the opportunity to contest the royalty award are moot.

B.    Respondents’ Request to Correct Arithmetic Error in the Final Award 

Respondents ask the Court to correct an “evident arithmetic error” pursuant to Code of Civil Procedure section 1286.6(a), which allows correction where: “There was an evident miscalculation of figures or an evident mistake in the description of any person, thing or property referred to in the award ….”

Respondents argue that: “The Award applies a 67.96% ownership percentage for Hola Comida Management LLC's [i.e., HCM’s] interest in Hola Comida Hospitality LLC [HCH].  [However,] Trial Exhibit 218— the 2025 cap table for [HCH]—shows HCM holds 21,771 Common Units out of 34,833 total Units outstanding, which equals 62.50%.  The 67.96% figure cannot be derived from Trial Exhibit 218 or any other exhibit in the record.  Substituting 62.50% for 67.96%, applied to the same enterprise value and multiplier the Arbitrator used, produces correct damages of $884,200—a reduction of $77,326.” (5/18/26 Response to Second Petition, pp. 5:25-6:5.)

However, as Petitioner argues, Respondents raised the ownership percentage argument before the Arbitrator, and the Arbitrator rejected it. (See 5/7/26 Escalante Decl., Exh. D -Respondents’ 3/10/26 Request for Correction, pp. 5:26-7:8 [“The Award cannot selectively rely on the HCH Agreement to establish Egan’s percentage of ownership while ignoring the same agreement’s provisions defining the economic value of that ownership. Indeed, the 67.96% figure the Award relies upon is itself inaccurate. The Membership Schedule to the HCH Agreement reflects that HCM holds 21,771 Common Units out of 34,833 total Units outstanding, a 62.50% interest, not 67.96%. Whether ruling the interest is 67.96%, or correctly ruling HCM’s interest in HCH is 62.50%, the straight-line application of the HCM interest to the enterprise value determined by Mr. Altstadt does not account for the distinction between Class A and Common Units and therefore overstates the value of HCM’s interest. Mr. Altstadt himself conceded that if ownership percentage information differed from his assumptions, his numbers “could — would have to be adjusted.’ [Citation]” (emphasis removed)]; 5/7/26 Escalante Decl., Exh. E -a copy of the Arbitrator’s 3/18/26 Ruling on Application for Correction of Award, p. 1 [“Respondents’ application is denied. It offers an analysis of the inter-relationship of two exhibits that were minimally referenced during the hearing, and about which little or no testimony was presented. Based upon this analysis, respondents seek reconsideration of the testimony and opinions of expert witness John Alstadt and propose that a different manner of damage calculation be adopted. Rather than advocating for correction of an evident miscalculation or an evident mistake in description of a person, thing, or property referred to in the Award, in effect, this application is for consideration of additional evidence, consideration of an interpretation of that evidence that was not presented at the hearing, and for the reweighing of the evidence that was”].)

The Court finds that Respondents are asking the Court to do more than fix a clear miscalculation of figures; they are asking the Court to reweigh the evidence and application of values. There is no statutory basis for that request.

Therefore, Respondents’ request for an order changing Gil’s ownership percentage is denied.

C.    Other Portions of the Final Award

Respondents have not challenged other portions of the Final Award. Therefore, the Court grants Petitioner’s request to confirm the entire Final Award except the vacated portions.

 

V.        CONCLUSION

The Petition to Confirm the Arbitration Award is GRANTED IN PART and DENIED IN PART as follows.

The request to confirm part of the arbitration award that awarded Claimant Joshua Gil the following remedies is GRANTED:

(a)   Ownership-Interest Damages of $961,526.00 from Mr. Egan, HCIII, HCH, and HCM, jointly and severally;

(b)   Costs of $16,232.99 from all Respondents, jointly and severally;

(c)   Post-Award, Pre-Judgment Interest of $9,823.47 at the rate of seven percent (7%) per annum (equating to $209.01 per day) from April 16, 2026 through the date hereof; and

(d)   Declaration that the Limited Partnership Agreement, dated January 2020, and executed by both Mr. Gil and Mr. Egan, is binding on Mr. Gil and Mr. Egan.

The petition is otherwise DENIED.

Moving Party is ordered to give notice and to file and serve, within 5 days of this ruling, a proposed order consistent with this ruling.

Case Number: 25STCV20094    Hearing Date: July 14, 2026    Dept: 730

Superior Court of California

County of Los Angeles

Department 730

 

MARITZA FONSECA,   

                         Plaintiff, 

vs. 

GENERAL MOTORS, LLC, et al., 

                         Defendants. 

Case No.:

25STCV20094

Hearing Date:

July 14, 2026

[TENTATIVE] ORDER OVERRULING DEMURRER

 

I.           BACKGROUND

            On June 30, 2025, plaintiff Martin Fonseca (“Plaintiff”) filed a complaint against defendant General Motors, LLC (“Defendant”) and DOES 1 through 10, inclusive.   

            On November 6, 2025, Defendant filed a demurrer to the complaint, which was set for hearing on February 10, 2026.  

            Prior to the hearing on the demurrer, on January 28, 2026, Plaintiff filed the operative first amended complaint (“FAC”) against Defendant and DOES 1 through 10, inclusive, alleging causes of action for: (1) Violation of Subdivision (D) of Civil Code section 1793.2; (2) Violation of Subdivision (B) of Civil Code section 1793.2; (3) Violation of Subdivision (A)(3) of Civil Code section 1793.2; (4) Breach of the Implied Warranty of Merchantability; and (5) Fraudulent Inducement—Concealment. This action arises from the sale and purchase of an allegedly defective 2019 GMC Terrain (the “Subject Vehicle”). (FAC, ¶ 6.)  

            On March 6, 2026, Defendant filed a demurrer to the FAC. On June 30, 2026, Plaintiff filed an opposition. On July 6, 2026, Defendant filed a reply.

II.         LEGAL STANDARD

Code of Civil Procedure[1] section 430.10 states: “The party against whom a complaint or cross-complaint has been filed may object, by demurrer or answer as provided in Section 430.30, to the pleading on any one or more of the following grounds: (a) The court has no jurisdiction of the subject of the cause of action alleged in the pleading; (b) The person who filed the pleading does not have the legal capacity to sue; (c) There is another action pending between the same parties on the same cause of action; (d) There is a defect or misjoinder of parties; (e) The pleading does not state facts sufficient to constitute a cause of action; (f) The pleading is uncertain. As used in this subdivision, uncertain includes ambiguous and unintelligible; and (g) in an action founded upon a contract, it cannot be ascertained from the pleading whether the contract is written, is oral, or is implied by conduct.”

As a general matter, in a demurrer proceeding, the defects must be apparent on the face of the pleading or via proper judicial notice.  (Donabedian v. Mercury Ins. Co. (2004) 116 Cal.App.4th 968, 994.)  “A demurrer tests the pleading alone, and not the evidence or facts alleged.”  (E-Fab, Inc. v. Accountants, Inc. Servs. (2007) 153 Cal.App.4th 1308, 1315.)  As such, the court assumes the truth of the complaint’s properly pleaded or implied factual allegations.  (Ibid.)  The only issue a demurrer is concerned with is whether the complaint, as it stands, states a cause of action.  (Hahn v. Mirda (2007) 147 Cal.App.4th 740, 747.)

Where a demurrer is sustained, leave to amend must be allowed where there is a reasonable possibility of successful amendment.  (Goodman v. Kennedy (1976) 18 Cal.3d 335, 348.)  The burden is on the plaintiff to show the court that a pleading can be amended successfully.  (Ibid.; Lewis v. YouTube, LLC (2015) 244 Cal.App.4th 118, 226.)  However, “[i]f there is any reasonable possibility that the plaintiff can state a good cause of action, it is error to sustain a demurrer without leave to amend.”  (Youngman v. Nevada Irrigation Dist. (1969) 70 Cal.2d 240, 245).

“[W]hile a statute of limitations normally sets the time within which proceedings must be commenced once a cause of action accrues, the statute of repose limits the time within which an action may be brought and is not related to accrual. Indeed, ‘the injury need not have occurred, much less have been discovered. Unlike an ordinary statute of limitations which begins running upon accrual of the claim, [the] period contained in a statute of repose begins when a specific event occurs, regardless of whether a cause of action has accrued or whether any injury has resulted.’ [Citation.] A statute of repose thus is harsher than a statute of limitations in that it cuts off a right of action after a specified period of time, irrespective of accrual or even notice that a legal right has been invaded. [Citation.]” (Giest v. Sequoia Ventures, Inc. (2000) 83 Cal.App.4th 300, 305.)

           

III.       DISCUSSION

A.             First through Third Causes of Action: Song Beverly Act

            Defendant demurs to the first through third causes of action under the Song-Beverly Act arguing they are time-barred by the statute of limitations and statute of repose. In opposition, Plaintiff argues that Code of Civil Procedure section 871.21 should not apply in this case because retroactive application is a violation of due process, the statute of limitations does not apply to inadequate literature/parts claims, and the action was filed prior to July 1, 2025.

 

1.     Retrospective Application

            “An action¿covered by Section 871.20 shall be commenced within one year after the expiration of the applicable express warranty.”¿ (Code Civ. Proc., § 871.21, subd. (a).)¿ Notwithstanding that deadline, “an action covered by Section 871.20 shall not be brought later than six years after the date of original delivery of the motor vehicle.”¿ (Code Civ. Proc., § 871.21, subd. (b).)¿ 

 

            Applying the statute retrospectively would create a due process issue. “[W]here the change in remedy, as, for example, the shortening of a time limit provision, is made retroactive, there must be a reasonable time¿permitted¿for the party affected to avail himself of his remedy before the statute takes effect. If the statute¿operates¿immediately¿to cut off the existing remedy, or within so short a time as to give the party no reasonable opportunity to exercise his remedy, then the retroactive application of it is unconstitutional as to such party.” (Rosefield Packing Co. v. Superior Court (1935) 4 Cal.2d 120, 122-123.) Moreover, there is a presumption against retroactive application unless there is express language or a clear and unavoidable implication¿that the Legislature intended retroactive application. (Quarry v. Doe I¿(2012) 53 Cal.4th 945, 955.)¿¿

 

            Here, Defendant argues the statute of repose began to run on October 2, 2018, when Plaintiff entered into a warranty contract for the Subject Vehicle. (FAC ¶ 6.) Six years from that date would be October 2, 2024. This action being filed on June 30, 2025, Defendant argues, makes the action untimely. As of January 1, 2025, there was no time left for Plaintiff to bring this action under section 871.20, subdivision (b), thus applying that section retroactively would violate Plaintiff’s due process rights. Moreover, given the presumption against retroactive legislation and there being no clear¿indication¿that the Legislature intended retroactivity, the Court declines retroactive application.

 

Therefore, Plaintiff’s first through third causes of action are not time-barred by the statute of repose.

 

2.     Statute of Limitations

            California courts have consistently held that claims under the¿Song-Beverly¿Act are governed by the four-year limitations period¿set forth in¿California Commercial Code section 2725.¿(Krieger v. Nick Alexander Imports, Inc.¿(1991)¿234 Cal.App.3d 205;¿Code Civ.¿Proc. §¿1790.) This statute provides that "an action for breach of any contract for sale must be commenced within four years after the cause of action has accrued."¿(Com.¿Code § 2725.)¿ 

 

            “Where a warranty explicitly extends to future performance of the goods and discovery of the breach must await the time of such performance the cause of action accrues when the breach is or should have been discovered."¿(Com. Code, § 2725.)¿¿ 

 

            Here, the Complaint alleges Plaintiff discovered Defendant’s wrongful conduct “shortly before the filing of the complaint,” which was on June 30, 2025. (FAC ¶ 29.) It does not “clearly and¿affirmatively appear on the face of the complaint that the action is barred by the statute of limitations.” (E-Fab, Inc. v. Accountants, Inc. Services¿(2007) 153 Cal.App.4th¿1308, 1326.)¿ Therefore, Plaintiff’s first through third causes of action are not time-barred by the statute of limitations.

 

Accordingly, Defendant’s demurrer to the first through third causes of action is OVERRULED.

 

B.              Fourth Cause of Action: Breach of Implied Warranty of Merchantability

Defendant demurs to Plaintiff’s fourth cause of action arguing it is time-barred by the statute of limitations.

 

            “The statute of limitations for breaches of the implied warranty of merchantability is four years.” (Montoya v. Ford Motor Co. (2020) 46 Cal.App.5th 493, 495.) A cause of action for breach of warranty occurs when the “tender of delivery is made, except where a warranty explicitly extends to future performance of the goods and discovery of the breach must await the time of such performance the cause of action accrues when the breach is or should have been discovered.” (Comm. Code section 2725, subd. (2).) As an implied warranty cannot explicitly extend to future performance of goods, the statute of limitation always runs from tender of delivery. (Cardinal Health 301, Inc. v. Tyco Elecs. Corp. (2008) 169 Cal.App.4th 116, 134.) 

 

            Plaintiff alleges the implied warranty accompanied the sale of the Subject Vehicle. (FAC ¶ 46.) Therefore, the point of accrual runs from the delivery of the vehicle. (Comm. Code section 2725, subd. (2).) Plaintiff does not allege when the Subject Vehicle was delivered. Plaintiff’s lack of alleged dates of delivery does not provide a basis for demurrer. The running of the statute must appear “clearly and affirmatively” from the face of the complaint; it is not enough that the complaint might be time-barred. (Committee for Green Foothills v. Santa Clara County Bd. of Supervisors (2010) 48 Cal. App. 4th 32, 42.) Therefore, based on the FAC’s allegations, the Court cannot conclude that Plaintiff’s fourth cause of action is time-barred.

 

            Accordingly, Defendant’s demurrer to the fourth cause of action is OVERRULED.

 

C.              Fifth Cause of Action: Fraudulent Inducement – Concealment

Defendant demurs to Plaintiff’s fifth cause of action arguing it is time-barred and Plaintiff fails to allege a transactional relationship giving rise to a duty to disclose.

1.           Statute of Limitations

            Under Code of Civ. Proc. section 338, subd. (d), an action based in fraud has a three-year statute of limitations accruing from “the discovery, by the aggrieved party, of the facts constituting the fraud or mistake.” A plaintiff must exercise reasonable diligence in discovering alleged fraud.  (Seelenfreund v. Terminix of Northern California, Inc. (1978) 84 Cal.App.3d 133, 136.) 

 

Plaintiff alleges he entered into the warranty contract on October 2, 2018. (FAC ¶ 6.) However, Plaintiff could not have reasonably discovered any alleged fraud prior to delivery of the Subject Vehicle. Plaintiff does not allege when the Subject Vehicle was delivered. Plaintiff alleges he discovered Defendant’s alleged wrongful conduct “shortly before the filing of the complaint,” which was on June 30, 2025. (FAC ¶ 29.) Therefore, Defendant’s argument that the FAC provides on its face a basis for demurrer on statute of limitations grounds is incorrect.

2.          Duty to Disclose

“The required elements for fraudulent concealment are (1) concealment or suppression of a material fact; (2) by a defendant with a duty to disclose the fact; (3) the defendant intended to defraud the plaintiff by intentionally concealing or suppressing the fact; (4) the plaintiff was unaware of the fact and would have acted differently if the concealed or suppressed fact was known; and (5) the plaintiff sustained damage as a result of the concealment or suppression of the material fact.” (Rattagan v. Uber Technologies, Inc. (2024) 17 Cal.5th 1, 40.)

Nondisclosure or concealment may constitute actionable fraud in four circumstances: (1) when the defendant is in a fiduciary relationship with the plaintiff; (2) when the defendant had exclusive knowledge of material facts not known to the plaintiff; (3) when the defendant actively conceals a material fact from the plaintiff; or (4) when the defendant makes partial representations but also suppresses some material fact.” (LiMandri v. Judkins (1997) 52 Cal.App.4th 326, 336.) A duty to disclose may also arise when a defendant possesses or exerts control over material facts not readily available to the plaintiff. (Jones v. ConocoPhillips Co. (2011) 198 Cal.App.4th 1198, 1199.)  

Defendant claims they had no duty to disclose because they had no fiduciary relationship with Plaintiff. Ordinarily, a duty to disclose absent a fiduciary relationship “presupposes the existence of [a] relationship between the plaintiff and defendant in which a duty to disclose can arise.” (Bigler-Engler v. Breg, Inc. (2017) 7 Cal.App.5th 276, 311.) However, a vendor has a duty to disclose material facts “not only to immediate purchasers, but also to subsequent purchasers when the vendor has reason to expect that the item will be resold.” (OCM Principle Opportunities Fund v. CIBC World Markets Corp. (2007) 157 Cal.App.4th 835, 859-860.)  The duty to disclose to subsequent purchasers is limited: the plaintiff must show that the seller had special “reason to expect” that the fraud will be passed onto subsequent purchasers. (Geernaert v. Mitchell (2007) 31 Cal.App.4th 601, 607-608.) Mere foreseeability is insufficient. (Id. [citing Restatement (Second) of Torts § 305, cmt. d (1977)].)  In determining whether the seller had “reason to expect” that the fraud will be passed onto subsequent purchasers, courts generally consider two factors: “(1) the extent of the seller’s knowledge of resale to a particular person or class of persons and (2) the likelihood that the particular misrepresentation (or concealment) would be passed on to them.” (Id. at 608.)

Here, the FAC alleges Defendant manufactured and/or distributed the Subject Vehicle, which Plaintiff purchased from an authorized dealer. (FAC ¶¶ 6, 8.) In addition, “Defendant GM had superior and exclusive knowledge of the Engine Defect and knew or should have known that the Engine Defect was not known or reasonably discoverable by Plaintiff before Plaintiff purchased the Subject Vehicle.” (FAC ¶ 61.) The FAC also alleges Defendant did not instruct dealerships to disclose defects to drivers or potential purchasers. (FAC ¶ 67.) Plaintiffs sufficiently allege facts showing Defendant had a reasonable expectation the fraud would be passed to subsequent purchasets. The pleadings have adequately pled Toyota’s duty of disclosure. Plaintiffs’ FAC adequately pleads facts to support a cause of action for fraudulent inducement – concealment.

Therefore, Defendant’s demurrer to the fifth cause of action is OVERRULED.

IV.        CONCLUSION

Defendant General Motor’s demurrer to Plaintiffs’ First Amended Complaint is OVERRULED.

Defendant is ordered to give notice.

Superior Court of California

JOANNA ALCOCER, an individual,

Plaintiff(s),

vs.

MERCEDES-BENZ USA, LLC, et al.,

Defendant(s).

Case No.:

26STCV08892

Hearing Date:

July 14, 2026

[TENTATIVE] ORDER RE:

MOTION TO COMPEL BINDING ARBITRATION AND MOTION TO STAY ACTION

 

I.         BACKGROUND

On March 19, 2026, Plaintiff Joana Alcocer (“Plaintiff”) filed this lemon law action against Defendants Mercedes-Benz USA, LLC (“MBUSA”), and Does 1 through 10, inclusive, alleging that her leased 2023 Mercedes-Benz GLC 300W was a new vehicle motor vehicle within the meaning of the Song Beverly Consumer Warranty Act, and MBUSA was unable to repair the vehicle’s defects during the warranty period despite reasonable opportunities to do so.

The Complaint asserts causes of action for: (1) violation of subdivision (d) of Civil Code section 1793.2; (2) violation of subdivision (b) of Civil Code section 1793.2; (3) violation of subdivision (a)(3) of Civil Code section 1793.2; and (4) breach of the implied warranty of merchantability.

On May 7, 2026, MBUSA filed the instant motion to compel Plaintiff’s claims to arbitration. On June 30, 2026, Plaintiff filed her opposition to the motion. On July 7, 2026, MBUSA filed its reply.

 

II.        LEGAL STANDARD

 “[A] court generally must compel arbitration in accordance with the agreement when requested by one of the parties. (Code Civ. Proc., § 1281.2; 9 U.S.C. § 2.)” (Ibid.) Under the FAA, “a written agreement to arbitrate ‘shall be valid, irrevocable, and enforceable, save upon such grounds as exist at law or in equity for the revocation of any contract ....’ (9 U.S.C. § 2.) Unless an exception applies, if the matter is arbitrable, the court ‘shall on application of one of the parties stay the trial of the action until such arbitration has been had in accordance with the terms of the agreement ....’ (9 U.S.C. § 3.)” (Ford Motor Warranty Cases (2025) 17 Cal.5th 1122, 1128 (Ford Motor Warranty Cases) [footnote removed].) 

“ ‘[I]n ruling on a motion to compel arbitration, the court must first determine whether the parties actually agreed to arbitrate the dispute. [Citations.] General principles of California contract law guide the court in making this determination.’ [Citation.] ‘The party seeking arbitration bears the burden of proving the existence of an arbitration agreement’ …. [Citation.]” (Ford Motor Warranty Cases, supra, 17 Cal.5th at p. 1128.)

“The moving party ‘can meet its initial burden by attaching to the petition a copy of the arbitration agreement purporting to bear the [opposing party’s] signature.’ [Citation.] Alternatively, the moving party can meet its burden by setting forth the agreement’s provisions in the motion. [Citations.] For this step, ‘it is not necessary to follow the normal procedures of document authentication.’ [Citation.]” (Gamboa v. Northeast Community Clinic (2021) 72 Cal.App.5th 158, 165 (Gamboa).)

“If the moving party meets its initial prima facie burden and the opposing party disputes the agreement, then in the second step, the opposing party bears the burden of producing evidence to challenge the authenticity of the agreement.” (Gamboa, supra, 72 Cal.App.5th at p. 165.) “The opposing party can do this in several ways. For example, the opposing party may testify under oath or declare under penalty of perjury that the party never saw or does not remember seeing the agreement, or that the party never signed or does not remember signing the agreement.” (Ibid.)

“The trial court sits as the trier of fact, weighing all the affidavits, declarations, and other documentary evidence, and any oral testimony the court may receive at its discretion, to reach a final determination.” (Ruiz v. Moss Bros. Auto Group, Inc. (2014) 232 Cal.App.4th 836, 842.)

 

III.      DISCUSSION

MBUSA moves to compel Plaintiff to arbitrate her claims pursuant to the arbitration agreement in the Lease Agreement of her vehicle. In her opposition, Plaintiff does not dispute MBUSA’s contentions that it is a third-party beneficiary under the arbitration agreement, and the FAA governs the agreement. Plaintiff only argues that the scope of the arbitration agreement does not cover her claims in this action.

“The FAA reflects a policy favoring arbitration, requiring that agreements to arbitrate be enforced in the same manner as any other contract.” (Ford Motor Warranty Cases, supra, 17 Cal.5th at p. 1128; but see Morgan v. Sundance, Inc. (2022) 596 U.S. 411, 418 [“The policy is to make ‘arbitration agreements as enforceable as other contracts, but not more so.’ [Citation.] Accordingly, a court must hold a party to its arbitration contract just as the court would to any other kind. But a court may not devise novel rules to favor arbitration over litigation. [Citation.] If an ordinary procedural rule—whether of waiver or forfeiture or what-have-you—would counsel against enforcement of an arbitration contract, then so be it. The federal policy is about treating arbitration contracts like all others, not about fostering arbitration”].)

“[S]tate contract rules generally govern the construction of arbitration agreements [governed by the FAA].” (Cronus Investments, Inc. v. Concierge Services (2005) 35 Cal.4th 376, 384.)

Under California law, “[t]he fundamental goal of contractual interpretation is to give effect to the mutual intention of the parties at the time of contract formation. (Civ. Code, § 1636.) ‘We ascertain that intention solely from the written contract if possible, but also consider the circumstances under which the contract was made and the matter to which it relates. [Citations.] We consider the contract as a whole and interpret the language in context, rather than interpret a provision in isolation. [Citation.] We interpret words in accordance with their ordinary and popular sense, unless the words are used in a technical sense or a special meaning is given to them by usage. [Citation.] If contractual language is clear and explicit and does not involve an absurdity, the plain meaning governs.’ ” (LaCour v. Marshalls of CA, LLC (2025) 117 Cal.App.5th 505, 521 (Lacourt).)

“When interpreting the provisions in an arbitration agreement covered by the FAA, due regard must be given to the federal policy favoring arbitration and, as a result, ambiguities as to the scope of the arbitration clause should be resolved in favor of arbitration. [Citations.]” (Lacourt, supra, 17 Cal.App.5th at p. 521; see also Mitsubishi Motors Corp. v. Soler Chrysler-Plymouth, Inc. (1985) 473 U.S. 614, 627 [“it is the congressional policy manifested in the Federal Arbitration Act that requires courts liberally to construe the scope of arbitration agreements covered by that Act …”].)

“ ‘At the same time, arbitration is a matter of consent, not coercion, and “ ‘a party cannot be required to submit to arbitration any dispute which he has not agreed so to submit’ ” [citation]. “[W]e do not override the clear intent of the parties, or reach a result inconsistent with the plain text of the contract, simply because the policy favoring arbitration is implicated.” ’ [Citation.]” (Lacourt, supra, 17 Cal.App.5th at p. 521.)

Here, the arbitration agreement states in relevant part:

“Any claim or dispute, whether in contract, tort or otherwise (including any dispute over the interpretation, scope, or validity of this lease, arbitration section or the arbitrability of any issue), between you and us or any of our employees, agents, successors, assigns, or the vehicle distributor, including Mercedes-Benz USA LLC (each a ‘Third Party Beneficiary’), which arises out of or relates to a credit application, this lease, or any resulting transaction or relationship arising out of this lease (including any such relationship with third parties who do not sign this contract) shall, at the election of either you, us, or a Third Party Beneficiary, be resolved by a neutral, binding arbitration and not by a court action.”

(Declaration of Sybil Leung, filed May 7, 2026, Exh. 1 – a copy of the Lease Agreement, p. 4, “Important Arbitration Disclosures” section, second paragraph [bold emphasis added].)

            MBUSA argues that Plaintiff’s claims arise out or relate to the Lease Agreement within the meaning of the above arbitration clause for the following reasons. “The relationship between MBUSA (the vehicle’s distributor and warrantor) and Plaintiff (the lessee) would not exist without the Lease between Plaintiff and the dealership (the lessor). Plaintiff, upon receiving the vehicle under the terms of the Lease, received an express warranty from MBUSA because Plaintiff leased the vehicle. As discussed in the moving brief, Plaintiff’s claims are brought under the Song-Beverly Act, which creates statutory claims arising out of retail purchases and leases of vehicles. [Citation.] Plaintiff’s claims arise out of the relationship between Plaintiff as lessee/consumer and MBUSA as distributor/warrantor. There would be no claim for breach of warranty under the Song-Beverly Act without this relationship, as Plaintiff’s claims in the complaint allege this action arises out of MBUSA’s warranty obligations, for a vehicle leased by Plaintiff, for which a written warranty was issued, and for which implied warranties arise by virtue of the Lease. In fact, Plaintiff acknowledges that both the express and implied warranties arise from the Lease: [¶] • ‘When the Subject Vehicle was leased, Plaintiff received express written warranties in which Defendant undertook to preserve or maintain the utility or performance of Subject Vehicle or to provide compensation if there is a failure in utility or performance for a specified period of time.’ (Compl. ¶ 11.) [¶] • ‘[T]he sale of Subject Vehicle was accompanied by Defendant’s implied warranty ….’ (Id. ¶ 30.) Simply put, there would be no warranties in the absence of the Lease”].)

 

When the parties to an arbitration agreement indicate that the agreement is ambiguous by disputing its meaning but, like here, fail to present extrinsic evidence in support of their arguments, California courts “resolve the question of ambiguity based solely on the contents of their agreement.” (Duran v. EmployBridge Holding Co. (2023) 92 Cal.App.5th 59, 66.)

Here, the Court finds that the language of the arbitration agreement does not cover Plaintiff’s claims for the following reasons.

It is true, as MBUSA argues, that Ford Motor Warranty Cases involved a slightly different arbitration agreement. There, “nothing in the agreement between plaintiffs and the seller dealers expressed an intent to empower third parties to invoke the arbitration clause.” (Ford Motor Warranty Cases, supra, 17 Cal.5th at p. 1129.) Here, the arbitration agreement clearly mentions MBUSA and defines the defendant as third party beneficiary under the agreement and contract in general.

However, Fort Motor Warranty Cases is relevant to the issue of scope.

Indeed, aside from the difference the Court has indicated above, the arbitration clause in that case was much broader than the language at issue. Specifically, the agreement stated that the contracting parties had agreed to arbitrate: “‘[a]ny claim or dispute, whether in contract, tort, statute or otherwise (including the interpretation and scope of this Arbitration Provision, and the arbitrability of the claims or dispute), between you and us or our employees, agents, successors or assigns, which arises out of or relates to your credit application, purchase, or condition of this vehicle, this contract or any resulting transaction or relationship (including any such relationship with third parties who did not sign this contract) ….” (Ford Motor Warranty Cases, supra, 17 Cal.5th at p. 1127 [bold and italicized emphasis added].)

The manufacturer (Ford Motor Company) argued that the above language covered plaintiffs’ Song-Beverly Warranty Consumer Act warranty claims and fraudulent concealment claim because those “claims [were] necessarily intertwined with the sales contracts ….” (Ford Motor Warranty Cases, supra, 17 Cal.5th at p. 1136.)

            The California Supreme Court disagreed, explaining that the “[p]laintiffs causes of action alleging warranty violations and fraud do not seek to enforce any contractual provision. As a result, they should not be estopped from pursuing their claims to court.” (Ford Motor Warranty Cases, supra, 17 Cal.5th at pp. 1130-1131; see also id. at p. 1138 [“In sum, Ford cannot compel plaintiffs to arbitrate their claims against it. Properly read, the language of the arbitration clauses agreed to by plaintiffs and the dealers does not support an agreement to arbitrate with third parties. Further, plaintiffs’ claims flow not from the contracts but from separate statutory requirements and conventional fraud theories. They are not intimately founded in and intertwined with the contractual terms”].)

Here, given the California Supreme Court’s holding in Ford Motor Warranty Cases, the Court finds that Plaintiff’s warranty claims do not “arise[] out of or relate[] to a credit application, [the] lease, or any resulting transaction or relationship arising out of [the] lease …” within the meaning of the arbitration agreement at issue.

Therefore, the Court denies MBUSA’s motion to compel Plaintiff’s claims to arbitration.

 

V.        CONCLUSION

The Motion to Compel Binding Arbitration and Motion to Stay Action is denied.

Plaintiff Joanna Alcocer to give notice.
